   Vice President JD Vance took the stage Thursday night at the GOP convention with a big smile on his face. A proud papa.

   By the time he was done speaking, roughly 40 minutes later, the crowd was riveted, enthralled, jubilant, ebullient, and—perhaps—looking for the first time to the future .

   Before Vance spoke, most of the speeches at the convention had focused on two things: praising President Trump and denigrating what other Republicans described as “crazy” Democrats.

   Republicans are trying hard to block Democrats from taking control of Congress in November. But Vance had a bigger message.

   He began by talking about his six-week old son, Alec, and the country that he wants Alec to grow up in. It was a hopeful vision, one that Vance said he holds for all young Americans, no matter their background. A lot of the convention before this had been doom and gloom. Vance was talking as a proud parent, and the crowd was loving it.

   Vance would later pivot. He invoked some of the more extreme statements from Democratic congressional candidates and said this is the risk Americans face if they don’t support Republicans in November. He said Democrats were “the party of hatred.”

   Tucked into his speech was an important appeal. He was speaking on the first anniversary of the assassination of his dear friend Charlie Kirk. He said he and Kirk, despite talking almost every day, had disagreements on U.S. foreign policy. And Vance asked young men, many of whom were huge Kirk fans, not to give up on the Republican Party just because they are mad about the war with Iran. This is a real sore point for the White House, and a real vulnerability for Republicans in November. It was an appeal the White House hadn’t articulated well before Thursday night.

   And so last night, Vance wasn’t hidden in Trump’s shadow. He was in the spotlight himself.

Damian Paletta
 
The Night JD Vance Stole the Show
 
Plus, Congress finally wakes up to the threats posed by AI, and the Supreme Court again blocks Missouri’s GOP-friendly voter map
 
 
JABIN BOTSFORD FOR WSJ
 

Good morning from Dallas.

 

Vice President JD Vance took the stage Thursday night at the GOP convention with a big smile on his face. A proud papa.

 

By the time he was done speaking, roughly 40 minutes later, the crowd was riveted, enthralled, jubilant, ebullient, and—perhaps—looking for the first time to the future.

 

Before Vance spoke, most of the speeches at the convention had focused on two things: praising President Trump and denigrating what other Republicans described as “crazy” Democrats.

 

Republicans are trying hard to block Democrats from taking control of Congress in November. But Vance had a bigger message.

 

He began by talking about his six-week old son, Alec, and the country that he wants Alec to grow up in. It was a hopeful vision, one that Vance said he holds for all young Americans, no matter their background. A lot of the convention before this had been doom and gloom. Vance was talking as a proud parent, and the crowd was loving it.

 

Vance would later pivot. He invoked some of the more extreme statements from Democratic congressional candidates and said this is the risk Americans face if they don’t support Republicans in November. He said Democrats were “the party of hatred.”

 

Tucked into his speech was an important appeal. He was speaking on the first anniversary of the assassination of his dear friend Charlie Kirk. He said he and Kirk, despite talking almost every day, had disagreements on U.S. foreign policy. And Vance asked young men, many of whom were huge Kirk fans, not to give up on the Republican Party just because they are mad about the war with Iran. This is a real sore point for the White House, and a real vulnerability for Republicans in November. It was an appeal the White House hadn’t articulated well before Thursday night.

 

And so last night, Vance wasn’t hidden in Trump’s shadow. He was in the spotlight himself.

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

September 11: Commemorations are being held in New York City, Washington, D.C., and Shanksville, Penn., on the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks.

 

Inflation: The Bureau of Labor Statistics will release August’s CPI report at 8.30 a.m. ET.

 

Trump’s Friday: The president and first lady Melania Trump will participate in a 9/11 Observance Ceremony at the Pentagon at 9 a.m. ET. He will later have a policy meeting at 3:30 p.m. ET.

What I’m Following

 
 
CORNELL WATSON/BLOOMBERG NEWS
 

Congress is finally waking up to the threats posed by AI. Dozens of lawmakers are calling for action to regulate AI after this week’s warnings that the technology could destroy humanity, but few agree on what those bills should look like, illustrating the gridlock that has left the industry largely free of government oversight. One obstacle: tons of AI money flowing to campaigns.

 

The Supreme Court again blocks Missouri’s Republican-friendly voter map. Justices blocked for a second time use of a congressional map in November’s midterm elections that the state GOP redrew to benefit the party. The court issued a brief order Thursday to end the dispute. No justices recorded any dissent, and the order came less than an hour after Missouri Republicans submitted a legal brief seeking to use their preferred map.

 

Iran has continued to make ballistic missiles. Iran has resumed production of missiles, assembling them from stored components into weapons in underground facilities, officials from the U.S. and Middle East familiar with the matter said. This is despite significant disruption to its manufacturing base and supply chain.

• A recovery in Middle East oil flows is expected to stretch into next year as escalating attacks on Gulf shipping and Houthi threats in the Red Sea keep key energy arteries under strain, the IEA said.

 

• California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed over a dozen bills Thursday regulating “addictive” social-media features and AI-driven chatbots.
